newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government in dilemma over immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: French government in dilemma over immigration bill.

text.p: The French government is on the horns of a dilemma over immigration.

Conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe faces the unenviable choice between alienating much of France's intellectual and artistic elite, as well as liberals in his own camp, and driving conservative voters into arms of the extreme right.
By mishandling an immigration bill now before parliament, he may yet achieve both, analysts say.

Juppe chose to yield to a torrent of protests from the left, civil libertarians and intellectuals, by agreeing this week to drop a clause requiring citizens to report to the police when foreign guests subject to visa requirements left their homes.
The measure was aimed at ensuring that visitors from Third World countries on short-term tourist visas do not overstay and swell the ranks of illegal immigrant workers.
Critics branded it shameful. Some likened it to the legal obligation to denounce the presence of Jews during the World War Two Nazi occupation of France and called for civil disobedience.

More than 15,000 performers, artists, writers, academics and professionals -- including household names such as actresses Catherine Deneuve and Jeanne Moreau -- have signed petitions denouncing the immigration bill.
The opposition Socialist and Communist parties have joined calls for a giant protest march in Paris on Saturday.
Yet just as the government resigned itself to an amendment leaving it to foreigners to report their own departure, a poll showed that 59 percent of voters backed its original proposal.
The IFOP survey in the left-wing daily Liberation found only 39 percent opposed forcing French hosts to report the movements of non-European foreigners, a clear -- if eminent -- minority.

The poll showed voters were almost evenly divided on the protest movement, with 49 percent disapproving of it and 48 percent approving. However a clear majority of 58 percent disapproved of calls for civil disobedience.
The extreme-right National Front was quick to accuse the government of capitulating to "show-biz well-to-do and the caviar left" and to demand a referendum on immigration.
The movement led by anti-immigration crusader Jean-Marie Le Pen has alarmed France's mainstream parties by capturing 15 percent of the vote and winning control of four southern towns.

It was with the intention of winning back right-wing voters from the Front that Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre proposed his bill to close loopholes in immigration law left by his equally tough predecessor, Charles Pasqua.
Pasqua's 1993 law had created absurd situations in which, for example, an illegal alien who had a child born in France could neither be expelled nor made a legal resident.
A cabinet minister said Debre set out to "cut the grass from beneath the National Front's feet". But critics, not just on the left, said he may have played into Le Pen's hands.

Opposition Socialist floor leader Laurent Fabius accused the government of making an issue of immigration to mask its failure to bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment, which polls show is the French people's number one concern.
Political sources said Juppe was reluctant from the outset to put forward Debre's bill and privately told visitors last November it would not see daylight in its original form.

To his dismay, right-wing government back-benchers hardened the legislation still further by passing amendments in a largely deserted National Assembly after most deputies, including most Socialists and Communists, had left for the Christmas holidays.

The government had the Senate (upper house) reject the harshest amendments, but the bill's return to the lower house became entangled with a municipal election in the southern town of Vitrolles, near Marseille, which the National Front won.
Now Juppe stands accused by the hard right of ineffectual "half-measures" on immigration, and by the left of making Third World visitors into scapegoats for France's economic ills.

"Ninety percent of illegal labour in France is done by French nationals and only 10 percent by foreigners. So it's a phoney problem," said Professor Leon Schwartzenberg, one of the leaders of the protest movement.
But Juppe is not the only one with a problem. The Socialist party, which put up only token resistance to the bill in December, was slow to join the protest movement.
The Socialists and Communists are also vying to win back from the National Front the support of working-class voters who live side-by-side with immigrants in difficult neighbourhoods.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin tied himself in knots by saying that while as a politician he could not urge people to disobey the law, as a private citizen, he could not imagine obeying such a law.
